There is therefore no bechina subgraph from which packages could be derived, and no bechina-defined concept clusters visible in the source text that would constitute candidate new packages.

The Torah's conceptual structure is entirely narrative and eitza-based:

1. PRINCIPLE (Baal Shem Tov): Before every decree in the world, the heavenly court gathers all creation — including the person upon whom the decree falls — and obtains their implicit consent by asking them about a parallel case. The person unwittingly renders the verdict against himself.

2. PROOF — King David and Nathan the Prophet (Samuel II, Ch. 12): Nathan tells the parable of the rich man who took the poor man's lamb. David declares 'As God lives, the man shall die!' — sealing his own decree as it left his mouth. This is the archetypal case of מִדַּעְתּוֹ וְשֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ.

3. PRACTICAL GUIDANCE: One must be extremely careful when hearing stories and parables — lofty matters are hidden within them. Never seal the judgment hastily; always examine and triple-check (שֶׁיְּשַׁנֶּה וִישַׁלֵּשׁ) before rendering a verdict, for this is a life-threatening matter (סַכָּנַת נְפָשׁוֹת).

4. PROOF — Berakhot 5a: When Rabbi Yochanan asked Rabbi Elazar 'Are afflictions dear to you?' and the answer was 'Neither they nor their reward' — Rabbi Yochanan said 'Give me your hand,' and lifted him up. The teaching: one can explicitly decline afflictions by giving one's hand as a formal declaration of non-consent.

All four moves are eitza (causal/narrative) connections. None of the key concepts — גְּזַר דִּין, דַּעְתּוֹ, סִפּוּרֵי דְּבָרִים, יִסּוּרִין, מִדַּעְתּוֹ — are declared to be bechinot of each other. The Torah teaches through analogy and narrative proof, not through ontological equivalences.
